title: Warm springs act like a 1.5-day later survey per 1 C in Breeding Bird Survey counts of 317 species (1966-2025); this phenology-detection artefact is real but too small to explain weak climate tracking
abstract: Question: the Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) counts each route once per year on a calendar date. In a warm spring the breeding cycle is earlier, so a warm spring must act like a later survey date. Does this phenology-detection artefact explain part of the weak climate tracking of bird communities? Data: 130,303 standard BBS runs on 5,319 US and Canadian routes (2026 release, 1966-2025), GHCN_CAMS April-May temperature anomalies, 317 species; UKBMS 2024 flight periods and site indices of 48 butterfly species with E-OBS temperature. Method: per-species models with route x observer and year fixed effects gave the within-route survey-date slope and the spring-anomaly response; a cross-fitted (odd/even years) random-effects meta-regression across species gave the implied phenological advance k. We wrote the plan before the outcomes. Results: species whose counts fall through the season had lower counts after warm springs. k was 1.45 days per 1 C (species bootstrap 1.19-1.72; permutation p = 0.001), 1.52 with migration, temperature-index and abundance covariates, 1.40 with family effects, and 1.24 from the within-species anomaly x date term. The previous spring (-0.07) and the next spring (-0.02) gave no relation. Residents gave 2.2 and migrants 1.3 days per 1 C (exploratory). The artefact explains about 20% of between-species variance in spring responses, but its effect on the community temperature index trend is +0.0003 C per decade, and survey-date drift adds -0.0011, against an observed 0.024 C per decade. In butterflies, flight dates advanced 3.9 days per 1 C, and an emulated single visit changed same-summer responses by 5-13% per 1 C, as much as the true response; the emulation showed that the count-based estimator recovers about 77% of k. Conclusion: the artefact is real and must be corrected in single-species weather responses, but it does not explain the tracking deficit. Limitations: correlational design, no breeding-date data, check terms after the survey gave small slopes (about one sixth of the main value), coarse temperature, Gaussian flight curves.

display.caption: Each point is one BBS species. x: change of the count per 10 days later survey date inside routes (odd years in panel 1). y: change of the count per +1 C April-May anomaly (even years in panel 1). Black: decile means with 95% intervals. Orange: cross-fitted random-effects meta-regression; the slope is the implied phenological advance in days per 1 C. The relation occurs for the same spring only; the previous spring and the next spring (placebo) give slopes near 0.

Implied phenological advance k (days per +1 C) with 95% intervals: main cross-fitted test, covariate and family controls, within-species estimate, migration classes and window variants (blue); placebo and check terms (orange). Variants below the within-species row use the full sample and are not cross-fitted.

citations.reason: Hearing-type observer drift and the within-observer CTI trend are the comparison scale for the new phenology-detection artefact; we use its BBS selection rules.
We reuse its species envelope rules and spatial-gradient estimator; we show that the small transient bird response is not mainly a single-visit phenology artefact.
Bird CTI followed less than 10% of warming; the phenology artefact does not explain this deficit.
Synthesis of 75 networks: weak tracking is a small temporal sensitivity; we rule out one detection cause of it in BBS.
Shows that the spatial denominator is mostly thermal, so detection causes of the temporal deficit are the open question.
